notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and use food and nutrients.
  • Human nutrition supplies energy, materials for growth and repair, and substances required for regulation of body functions.
  • A balanced diet contains all essential nutrients in appropriate amounts.
  • Major nutrients include carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.
  • Dietary fibre is also essential for healthy digestive function.
  • Nutrient requirements vary with age, sex, body size, physical activity, pregnancy, lactation and health status.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nutrition → Energy + Growth + Repair + Regulation

2. Nutrients

Nutrients are substances required by the body for:

  • Energy.
  • Growth.
  • Tissue repair.
  • Metabolism.
  • Immune function.
  • Maintenance of normal physiology.

Major nutrient groups are:

  • Carbohydrates.
  • Proteins.
  • Fats.
  • Vitamins.
  • Minerals.
  • Water.
3. Macronutrients

Macronutrients are required in relatively large amounts.

They include:

  • Carbohydrates.
  • Proteins.
  • Fats.

Water is also required in large quantities but does not provide energy.

4. Micronutrients

Micronutrients are required in smaller quantities.

They include:

  • Vitamins.
  • Minerals.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Micronutrient → Required in small amount.

It does not mean unimportant nutrient.

5. Balanced Diet
  • A balanced diet provides all essential nutrients in suitable proportions.
  • It should provide sufficient energy without chronic excess.
  • It should include adequate protein, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water.
  • Variety improves the likelihood of meeting micronutrient requirements.
6. Energy-Giving Nutrients

The main energy-yielding nutrients are:

  • Carbohydrates.
  • Fats.
  • Proteins.
  • Alcohol also provides energy but is not an essential nutrient.
7. Energy Values of Macronutrients

Approximate physiological energy values are:

  • Carbohydrate → 4 kcal/g.
  • Protein → 4 kcal/g.
  • Fat → 9 kcal/g.
📌 Must-Memorise

Carbohydrate → 4 kcal/g

Protein → 4 kcal/g

Fat → 9 kcal/g

8. Kilocalorie
  • Food energy is commonly expressed in kilocalories.
  • 1 kilocalorie is approximately 4.184 kilojoules.
  • A food “Calorie” with capital C generally means one kilocalorie.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 kcal ≈ 4.184 kJ

9. Carbohydrates
  • Carbohydrates are major sources of dietary energy.
  • They contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
  • Glucose is an important cellular fuel.
  • Carbohydrates are classified as simple and complex carbohydrates.
10. Monosaccharides

Important monosaccharides include:

  • Glucose.
  • Fructose.
  • Galactose.
  • They are simple sugars that do not need to be broken into smaller carbohydrate units before absorption.
11. Glucose
  • Glucose is a major fuel for cells.
  • Blood transports glucose to tissues.
  • Brain tissue relies heavily on glucose under ordinary dietary conditions.
  • Excess glucose can be stored as glycogen or converted into fat.
12. Fructose
  • Fructose occurs naturally in fruits and honey.
  • It is a monosaccharide.
  • It is sweeter than glucose.
13. Galactose
  • Galactose is a component of lactose.
  • Lactose digestion releases glucose and galactose.
14. Disaccharides

Important disaccharides include:

  • Sucrose.
  • Lactose.
  • Maltose.
15. Sucrose
  • Sucrose is common table sugar.
  • It consists of glucose + fructose.
  • Sugarcane and sugar beet are major commercial sources.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sucrose → Glucose + Fructose

16. Lactose
  • Lactose is commonly called milk sugar.
  • It consists of glucose + galactose.
  • Lactase enzyme digests lactose.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lactose → Milk Sugar

17. Maltose
  • Maltose consists of two glucose units.
  • It is formed during starch digestion.
  • Maltase converts maltose into glucose.
18. Polysaccharides

Important polysaccharides include:

  • Starch.
  • Glycogen.
  • Cellulose.
19. Starch
  • Starch is the major storage carbohydrate of plants.
  • It is abundant in rice, wheat, maize, potato and other cereals/tubers.
  • Starch is made of many glucose units.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Plant Storage Carbohydrate → Starch

20. Glycogen
  • Glycogen is the main storage carbohydrate in animals.
  • It is stored mainly in liver and skeletal muscles.
  • Liver glycogen helps maintain blood glucose.
  • Muscle glycogen provides local fuel for muscle activity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Animal Storage Carbohydrate → Glycogen

21. Cellulose
  • Cellulose forms plant cell walls.
  • Humans cannot digest cellulose because we lack cellulase.
  • Cellulose contributes to dietary fibre.
  • It helps bowel movement.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Humans cannot digest cellulose.

22. Dietary Fibre

Dietary fibre includes plant components resistant to digestion in the small intestine.

Functions include:

  • Increasing stool bulk.
  • Supporting bowel movement.
  • Helping prevent constipation.
  • Supporting healthy gut microbes.
  • Slowing glucose absorption in some foods.
  • Helping lower LDL cholesterol when soluble fibre is consumed.
23. Soluble Fibre

Sources include:

  • Oats.
  • Barley.
  • Pulses.
  • Fruits.
  • Psyllium.
  • Soluble fibre can form gels.
  • It may help control blood glucose and cholesterol.
24. Insoluble Fibre

Sources include:

  • Whole grains.
  • Bran.
  • Many vegetables.
  • Fruit skins.
  • Insoluble fibre increases stool bulk and supports intestinal movement.
25. Protein
  • Proteins are essential for growth and tissue repair.
  • They form enzymes, antibodies, many hormones and structural components.
  • Proteins are composed of amino acids.
  • Peptide bonds join amino acids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Protein → Amino Acids

26. Amino Acids
  • About 20 standard amino acids are commonly incorporated into human proteins.
  • Some can be synthesised adequately by the body.
  • Others must be obtained from food and are called essential amino acids.
27. Essential Amino Acids

For adults, the nine amino acids generally considered essential are:

  • Histidine.
  • Isoleucine.
  • Leucine.
  • Lysine.
  • Methionine.
  • Phenylalanine.
  • Threonine.
  • Tryptophan.
  • Valine.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Essential Amino Acids → Must Come from Diet

28. Complete Protein
  • A complete protein provides all essential amino acids in adequate proportions.
  • Eggs, milk, fish and meat are high-quality complete proteins.
  • Soy protein is also generally considered a complete plant protein.
29. Complementary Proteins
  • Different plant proteins can complement one another.
  • Cereals are often relatively low in lysine.
  • Pulses are often relatively low in methionine.
  • Combining cereals and pulses improves overall amino-acid balance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cereal + Pulse → Better Protein Quality

Examples:

Rice + dal.

Idli/dosa + sambar.

Chapati + dal.

30. Protein Sources

Animal sources:

  • Egg.
  • Milk.
  • Fish.
  • Meat.

Plant sources:

  • Pulses.
  • Lentils.
  • Soybeans.
  • Groundnuts.
  • Nuts.
  • Seeds.
31. Protein Deficiency
  • Severe protein deficiency can impair growth.
  • Muscle wasting may occur.
  • Immune function may decline.
  • Protein-energy malnutrition includes kwashiorkor and marasmus.
32. Kwashiorkor
  • Kwashiorkor is severe protein-energy malnutrition classically associated with inadequate protein intake.
  • Oedema is a characteristic feature.
  • Growth failure occurs.
  • Muscle wasting may be present.
  • Fatty liver can occur.
  • Hair and skin changes may develop.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kwashiorkor → Oedema

33. Marasmus
  • Marasmus results from severe deficiency of total energy and nutrients.
  • It causes extreme wasting.
  • Subcutaneous fat is markedly reduced.
  • Oedema is usually absent.
📌 Must-Memorise

Marasmus → Severe Wasting, Usually No Oedema

34. Kwashiorkor vs Marasmus

Kwashiorkor:

  • Oedema prominent.
  • Protein deficiency is classically emphasised.

Marasmus:

  • Severe calorie and protein deficiency.
  • Marked wasting.
  • Usually no oedema.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Oedema → Think Kwashiorkor.

35. Fats
  • Fats are concentrated sources of energy.
  • They provide 9 kcal/g.
  • They form cell membranes.
  • They provide essential fatty acids.
  • They help absorb fat-soluble vitamins.
  • They provide insulation and protect organs.
36. Triglycerides
  • Most dietary and stored fats are triglycerides.
  • A triglyceride consists of glycerol and three fatty acids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Triglyceride → Glycerol + 3 Fatty Acids

37. Saturated Fat
  • Saturated fatty acids contain no carbon-carbon double bonds.
  • They are common in butter, ghee, fatty meat and some tropical oils.
  • Excessive saturated-fat intake can raise LDL cholesterol in many people.
38. Unsaturated Fat
  • Unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds.
  • They are common in vegetable oils, nuts, seeds and fish.
  • Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats are major categories.
39. Monounsaturated Fat
  • Monounsaturated fatty acids contain one double bond.
  • Oleic acid is a common example.
  • Olive oil and groundnut oil contain substantial monounsaturated fat.
40. Polyunsaturated Fat
  • Polyunsaturated fatty acids contain multiple double bonds.
  • Omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids belong to this category.
  • Some are essential nutrients.
41. Essential Fatty Acids

Important essential fatty acids are:

  • Linoleic acid → Omega-6.
  • Alpha-linolenic acid → Omega-3.
  • The human body cannot synthesise them in sufficient amounts.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Essential Fatty Acids → Linoleic + Alpha-Linolenic

42. Omega-3 Fatty Acids
  • Alpha-linolenic acid is an essential plant omega-3 fatty acid.
  • EPA and DHA are long-chain omega-3 fatty acids.
  • Fatty fish are important sources of EPA and DHA.
  • Flaxseed and chia provide alpha-linolenic acid.
43. Trans Fat
  • Trans fats can form during partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
  • Some trans fats also occur naturally in small quantities in ruminant foods.
  • Industrial trans fats increase cardiovascular risk.
  • They tend to increase LDL and decrease HDL cholesterol.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Trans Fat → Cardiovascular Risk ↑

44. Cholesterol
  • Cholesterol is a sterol.
  • It is present in animal tissues.
  • It is a component of cell membranes.
  • It is a precursor for steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D.
  • The body can synthesise cholesterol.
45. LDL
  • LDL stands for low-density lipoprotein.
  • It transports cholesterol from liver to tissues.
  • Elevated LDL cholesterol is strongly associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LDL → Commonly Called “Bad” Cholesterol

46. HDL
  • HDL stands for high-density lipoprotein.
  • It participates in reverse cholesterol transport toward the liver.
  • Higher HDL levels are generally associated with lower cardiovascular risk, though cardiovascular assessment is more complex than HDL alone.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

HDL → Commonly Called “Good” Cholesterol

47. Vitamins
  • Vitamins are organic compounds required in small quantities for normal metabolism.
  • Most vitamins cannot be synthesised adequately by the body.
  • They do not directly provide energy.
  • They regulate many biochemical processes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Vitamins → No caloric energy.

48. Vitamin Classification

Fat-soluble vitamins:

  • A.
  • D.
  • E.
  • K.

Water-soluble vitamins:

  • B-complex.
  • C.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fat Soluble → A D E K

49. Fat-Soluble Vitamins
  • Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed with dietary fat.
  • They can be stored in body tissues.
  • Excess intake can produce toxicity more readily than many water-soluble vitamins.
50. Water-Soluble Vitamins
  • Most water-soluble vitamins are not stored extensively.
  • Excess amounts are often excreted in urine.
  • Vitamin B12 is an important exception because substantial stores can be maintained for years.
51. Vitamin A
  • Vitamin A is important for vision.
  • It maintains epithelial tissues.
  • It supports immune function and growth.
  • Retinol is an active vitamin A form.
  • Beta-carotene is a provitamin A carotenoid.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vitamin A → Vision

52. Vitamin A Sources

Sources include:

  • Liver.
  • Egg yolk.
  • Dairy products.
  • Carrot.
  • Pumpkin.
  • Green leafy vegetables.
  • Mango.
  • Papaya.
  • Orange and green plant foods often supply beta-carotene.
53. Vitamin A Deficiency

Major consequences include:

  • Night blindness.
  • Xerophthalmia.
  • Bitot spots.
  • Corneal damage in severe deficiency.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vitamin A Deficiency → Night Blindness

54. Xerophthalmia
  • Xerophthalmia is a spectrum of eye changes caused by severe vitamin A deficiency.
  • Dryness of conjunctiva and cornea can occur.
  • Severe cases may cause blindness.
55. Vitamin D
  • Vitamin D promotes calcium and phosphate absorption.
  • It is essential for normal bone mineralisation.
  • Skin can synthesise vitamin D when exposed to suitable ultraviolet-B radiation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vitamin D → Calcium + Bone

56. Vitamin D Forms

Important forms include:

  • Vitamin D₂ → Ergocalciferol.
  • Vitamin D₃ → Cholecalciferol.
57. Vitamin D Deficiency
  • In children, severe deficiency causes rickets.
  • In adults, it causes osteomalacia.
  • Bones become inadequately mineralised.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vitamin D Deficiency:

Children → Rickets

Adults → Osteomalacia

58. Rickets
  • Rickets affects growing bones.
  • Bowing of legs may occur.
  • Bone growth plates become abnormal.
  • Calcium/phosphate deficiency or vitamin D deficiency can contribute.
59. Vitamin E
  • Vitamin E functions mainly as a lipid-soluble antioxidant.
  • Alpha-tocopherol is an important form.
  • It protects cell membranes from oxidative damage.
  • Deficiency is uncommon but can occur with severe fat malabsorption.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vitamin E → Antioxidant

60. Vitamin K
  • Vitamin K is essential for normal synthesis of several clotting factors.
  • It is also involved in bone proteins.
  • Deficiency increases bleeding tendency.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vitamin K → Blood Clotting

61. Vitamin K and Newborns
  • Newborn babies have relatively low vitamin K stores.
  • Vitamin K prophylaxis is commonly given after birth to prevent vitamin-K-deficiency bleeding.
62. Vitamin B1
  • Vitamin B1 is thiamine.
  • It is important in carbohydrate metabolism and nerve function.
  • Deficiency causes beriberi.
📌 Must-Memorise

B1 → Thiamine → Beriberi

63. Beriberi

Two major forms are:

  • Dry beriberi → Mainly neurological.
  • Wet beriberi → Mainly cardiovascular and oedematous.
  • Severe thiamine deficiency can also cause Wernicke-Korsakoff neurological syndromes.
64. Vitamin B2
  • Vitamin B2 is riboflavin.
  • It forms coenzymes FAD and FMN.
  • It is involved in energy metabolism.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

B2 → Riboflavin

65. Riboflavin Deficiency

Possible signs include:

  • Cracks at corners of mouth.
  • Glossitis.
  • Dermatitis.
  • Angular cheilitis is a classic exam association.
66. Vitamin B3
  • Vitamin B3 is niacin.
  • It is required for NAD and NADP coenzymes.
  • Deficiency causes pellagra.
📌 Must-Memorise

B3 → Niacin → Pellagra

67. Pellagra

Classic “3 Ds”:

  • Dermatitis.
  • Diarrhoea.
  • Dementia.

Untreated severe disease may lead to death.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pellagra → 3D

68. Vitamin B5
  • Vitamin B5 is pantothenic acid.
  • It is a component of coenzyme A.
  • Deficiency is rare because it is widely distributed in foods.
69. Vitamin B6
  • Vitamin B6 includes pyridoxine-related compounds.
  • It is important in amino-acid metabolism.
  • It is involved in neurotransmitter and haemoglobin synthesis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

B6 → Pyridoxine

70. Vitamin B7
  • Vitamin B7 is biotin.
  • It functions in carboxylation reactions.
  • Deficiency is uncommon.
71. Vitamin B9
  • Vitamin B9 is folate/folic acid.
  • It is required for DNA synthesis and cell division.
  • Demand rises during pregnancy.
  • Adequate folate helps prevent neural-tube defects.
📌 Must-Memorise

B9 → Folate → Neural-Tube Defect Prevention

72. Folate Deficiency
  • Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia.
  • Rapidly dividing tissues are especially affected.
  • Pregnancy deficiency increases neural-tube-defect risk.
73. Vitamin B12
  • Vitamin B12 is cobalamin.
  • It contains cobalt.
  • It is essential for DNA synthesis, red-cell formation and nervous-system function.
  • Reliable natural dietary sources are mainly animal-derived foods.
📌 Must-Memorise

B12 → Cobalamin → Cobalt

74. Vitamin B12 Absorption
  • Vitamin B12 requires intrinsic factor for efficient absorption.
  • Intrinsic factor is produced by gastric parietal cells.
  • B12 is absorbed mainly in the terminal ileum.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

B12 → Intrinsic Factor → Ileum

75. Vitamin B12 Deficiency
  • B12 deficiency can cause megaloblastic anaemia.
  • Neurological symptoms may occur.
  • Pernicious anaemia results from impaired intrinsic-factor-related B12 absorption.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Folate deficiency and B12 deficiency can both cause megaloblastic anaemia, but neurological symptoms are particularly associated with B12 deficiency.

76. Vitamin C
  • Vitamin C is ascorbic acid.
  • It is required for collagen synthesis.
  • It enhances absorption of non-haem iron.
  • It acts as an antioxidant.
  • Humans cannot synthesise vitamin C.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vitamin C → Collagen + Iron Absorption

77. Vitamin C Sources

Important sources include:

  • Amla.
  • Guava.
  • Citrus fruits.
  • Tomato.
  • Capsicum.
  • Many fresh fruits and vegetables.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Amla/Guava → Rich Vitamin C Sources

78. Vitamin C Deficiency
  • Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.
  • Symptoms include bleeding gums.
  • Poor wound healing may occur.
  • Easy bruising can occur.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vitamin C → Scurvy

79. Important Vitamin-Deficiency Pairs
  • A → Night blindness.
  • B1 → Beriberi.
  • B3 → Pellagra.
  • B9 → Megaloblastic anaemia/neural-tube risk.
  • B12 → Megaloblastic anaemia + neurological problems.
  • C → Scurvy.
  • D → Rickets/osteomalacia.
  • K → Bleeding tendency.
80. Minerals
  • Minerals are inorganic elements required for normal body functions.
  • Major minerals are required in relatively larger quantities.
  • Trace minerals are required in smaller quantities.
81. Major Minerals

Important major minerals include:

  • Calcium.
  • Phosphorus.
  • Sodium.
  • Potassium.
  • Magnesium.
  • Chloride.
82. Trace Minerals

Important trace elements include:

  • Iron.
  • Iodine.
  • Zinc.
  • Copper.
  • Selenium.
  • Fluoride.
  • Manganese.
83. Calcium
  • Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body.
  • Most body calcium is stored in bones and teeth.
  • Calcium is also required for muscle contraction, nerve function and blood clotting.
📌 Must-Memorise

Most Abundant Body Mineral → Calcium

84. Calcium Sources

Sources include:

  • Milk and dairy products.
  • Ragi.
  • Sesame seeds.
  • Small fish eaten with bones.
  • Green leafy vegetables.
  • Fortified foods.
85. Calcium Deficiency
  • Severe deficiency contributes to poor bone mineralisation.
  • Long-term inadequate calcium can contribute to osteoporosis risk.
  • Muscle and nerve functions may also be affected.
86. Osteoporosis
  • Osteoporosis is characterised by reduced bone mass and increased fracture risk.
  • Risk rises with age.
  • Calcium, vitamin D, physical activity and hormones influence bone health.
  • Osteoporosis is not simply identical to vitamin D-deficiency rickets.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rickets → Defective mineralisation in growing children.

Osteoporosis → Reduced bone mass/strength.

87. Phosphorus
  • Phosphorus is important in bones and teeth.
  • It forms part of ATP.
  • It is present in DNA and RNA.
  • Phospholipids contain phosphorus.
88. Iron
  • Iron is essential for haemoglobin.
  • It also occurs in myoglobin and many enzymes.
  • Iron deficiency impairs oxygen transport.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Iron → Haemoglobin

89. Iron Deficiency Anaemia
  • Iron deficiency is a major cause of nutritional anaemia.
  • Haemoglobin concentration decreases.
  • Symptoms may include fatigue, weakness and pallor.
  • Children and menstruating/pregnant women are at higher risk.
📌 Must-Memorise

Iron Deficiency → Anaemia

90. Haem Iron
  • Haem iron occurs mainly in animal foods.
  • It is generally absorbed more efficiently than non-haem iron.
  • Meat and fish provide haem iron.
91. Non-Haem Iron
  • Non-haem iron occurs in plant foods and fortified foods.
  • Pulses and green leafy vegetables supply non-haem iron.
  • Vitamin C improves non-haem iron absorption.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vitamin C → Iron Absorption ↑

92. Iodine
  • Iodine is required for synthesis of thyroid hormones.
  • Thyroid hormones regulate metabolism and development.
  • Iodised salt is an important public-health source.
📌 Must-Memorise

Iodine → Thyroid Hormones

93. Iodine Deficiency
  • Iodine deficiency can cause goitre.
  • Severe deficiency during pregnancy and early life can impair brain development.
  • Iodine Deficiency Disorders is the broader public-health term.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Iodine Deficiency → Goitre

94. Goitre
  • Goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland.
  • Iodine deficiency is an important cause.
  • Goitre can also have other causes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

All goitre is not necessarily due to iodine deficiency.

95. Sodium
  • Sodium is the major extracellular cation.
  • It helps regulate fluid balance.
  • It is required for nerve impulses and muscle contraction.
  • Excessive sodium intake is associated with increased blood pressure in susceptible populations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Major Extracellular Cation → Sodium

96. Potassium
  • Potassium is the major intracellular cation.
  • It is essential for nerve and muscle function.
  • It contributes to normal heart rhythm.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Major Intracellular Cation → Potassium

97. Chloride
  • Chloride is the major extracellular anion.
  • It contributes to fluid balance.
  • Chloride is part of hydrochloric acid in gastric juice.
98. Magnesium
  • Magnesium participates in hundreds of enzyme reactions.
  • It is important for ATP-dependent processes.
  • It contributes to bone, muscle and nerve function.
99. Zinc
  • Zinc is required for many enzymes.
  • It supports growth, immunity and wound healing.
  • Severe deficiency can impair growth and taste.
100. Selenium
  • Selenium is an essential trace element.
  • It forms part of antioxidant enzymes such as glutathione peroxidase.
  • Both deficiency and excess can be harmful.
101. Fluoride
  • Fluoride strengthens tooth enamel and helps prevent dental caries at appropriate exposure.
  • Excessive fluoride intake can cause fluorosis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fluoride:

Adequate → Dental Caries ↓

Excess → Fluorosis

102. Dental Fluorosis
  • Excess fluoride during tooth development can cause mottling or discolouration of enamel.
  • Severe long-term excess exposure may affect bones.
103. Water
  • Water is essential for life.
  • It is the major component of the human body.
  • It transports nutrients and wastes.
  • It regulates temperature.
  • It acts as a solvent and participates in biochemical reactions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Water provides no calories.

104. Body Water
  • Total body water commonly makes up roughly 50–70% of adult body mass.
  • Percentage varies with age, sex and body composition.
  • Infants generally have a higher body-water percentage than older adults.
105. Dehydration
  • Dehydration occurs when water loss exceeds intake.
  • Symptoms may include thirst, dry mouth, dizziness and reduced urine output.
  • Severe dehydration can impair circulation and organ function.
106. Oral Rehydration Solution
  • ORS stands for Oral Rehydration Solution.
  • It treats dehydration caused by diarrhoea and similar fluid losses.
  • It contains glucose and electrolytes in appropriate concentrations.
  • Glucose facilitates sodium absorption in the intestine.
  • Water follows absorbed sodium.
📌 Must-Memorise

ORS → Glucose + Salts + Water

107. ORS Mechanism
  • Sodium-glucose cotransport remains functional in many diarrhoeal illnesses.
  • Glucose helps sodium enter intestinal cells.
  • Water follows osmotically.
  • ORS saves lives by restoring fluids and electrolytes.
108. Digestion of Carbohydrates
  • Carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth.
  • Salivary amylase acts on starch.
  • Pancreatic amylase continues starch digestion in small intestine.
  • Brush-border enzymes convert disaccharides into monosaccharides.
109. Carbohydrate Absorption
  • Monosaccharides are absorbed mainly in the small intestine.
  • Glucose and galactose use sodium-dependent transport.
  • Fructose uses facilitated transport.
  • Monosaccharides enter portal blood and travel to liver.
110. Protein Digestion
  • Protein digestion begins mainly in the stomach.
  • Pepsin breaks proteins into peptides.
  • Pancreatic proteases continue digestion in small intestine.
  • Peptidases produce amino acids and small peptides.
111. Protein Absorption
  • Amino acids and small peptides are absorbed through intestinal cells.
  • They enter portal circulation.
  • The liver processes absorbed amino acids.
112. Fat Digestion
  • Most fat digestion occurs in the small intestine.
  • Bile salts emulsify fat.
  • Pancreatic lipase breaks triglycerides down.
  • Products form micelles with bile salts.
113. Fat Absorption
  • Lipid products enter intestinal cells.
  • Long-chain fats are reassembled into triglycerides.
  • They are packaged into chylomicrons.
  • Chylomicrons enter lymphatic lacteals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dietary Fat → Chylomicrons → Lacteals

114. Basal Metabolic Rate
  • BMR stands for Basal Metabolic Rate.
  • It is the minimum energy expenditure required to maintain vital functions at rest under standard conditions.
  • BMR supports breathing, circulation, ion transport and other essential processes.
115. Factors Affecting BMR

BMR varies with:

  • Age.
  • Sex.
  • Body size.
  • Lean body mass.
  • Hormones.
  • Fever.
  • Pregnancy.
  • Environmental temperature.
116. Total Energy Expenditure

Daily energy expenditure includes:

  • Basal metabolism.
  • Physical activity.
  • Thermic effect of food.
  • Additional physiological needs such as growth or pregnancy.
117. BMI
  • BMI stands for Body Mass Index.
  • It is calculated using body weight and height.
📌 Formula

BMI = Weight in kg / Height² in metres

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

BMI Unit → kg/m²

118. Adult BMI Categories — General WHO Cut-offs
  • Underweight → Below 18.5.
  • Normal range → 18.5–24.9.
  • Overweight → 25.0–29.9.
  • Obesity → 30 or above.
📌 TNPSC Note

BMI does not directly measure body-fat percentage and is interpreted differently in children, pregnancy and some population-specific guidelines.

119. Malnutrition
  • Malnutrition includes undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, overweight and obesity.
  • It is not limited to starvation.
  • A person can consume excess calories while still lacking essential micronutrients.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Malnutrition ≠ Only undernutrition.

120. Undernutrition

Undernutrition may manifest as:

  • Underweight.
  • Wasting.
  • Stunting.
  • Micronutrient deficiencies.
121. Stunting
  • Stunting means low height for age in children.
  • It reflects chronic or repeated undernutrition and other adverse conditions.
  • It is a long-term indicator.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stunting → Low Height for Age

122. Wasting
  • Wasting means low weight for height.
  • It reflects acute undernutrition or severe recent weight loss.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Wasting → Low Weight for Height

123. Underweight
  • Underweight in children generally refers to low weight for age.
  • It can reflect both chronic and acute nutritional problems.
📌 Memory

Stunting → Height for age

Wasting → Weight for height

Underweight → Weight for age

124. Obesity
  • Obesity is excessive accumulation of body fat that increases health risks.
  • Energy intake chronically exceeding energy expenditure contributes to weight gain.
  • Genetics, environment, sleep, medications, hormones and activity also influence obesity.
125. Hidden Hunger
  • Hidden hunger refers to micronutrient deficiency despite apparently adequate calorie intake.
  • Common deficiencies include iron, iodine, vitamin A, zinc and folate deficiencies.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hidden Hunger → Micronutrient Deficiency

126. Anaemia
  • Anaemia is a condition in which blood has insufficient haemoglobin or red-cell capacity to carry oxygen adequately.
  • Iron deficiency is a common nutritional cause.
  • Folate and vitamin B12 deficiencies can also cause anaemia.
127. Food Fortification
  • Fortification adds micronutrients to commonly consumed foods.
  • It helps prevent population-wide deficiencies.
  • Iodised salt is a classic example.
  • Iron, folic acid, vitamin D and vitamin A may also be used in fortification programmes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Iodised Salt → Food Fortification

128. Iodised Salt
  • Iodised salt is fortified with iodine compounds.
  • It helps prevent iodine-deficiency disorders.
  • Iodine content can decrease with prolonged exposure to moisture, heat and improper storage.
129. Enrichment
  • Enrichment generally restores nutrients lost during food processing.
  • Fortification may add nutrients beyond the level naturally present.
  • The terms sometimes overlap in public-health usage.
130. Food Adulteration
  • Food adulteration is addition, substitution or removal of substances that lowers food quality or safety.
  • Adulterants may be intentional or accidental.
  • Adulteration can reduce nutrition or cause toxicity.
131. Food Preservation

Common preservation methods include:

  • Refrigeration.
  • Freezing.
  • Drying.
  • Salting.
  • Sugaring.
  • Pickling.
  • Canning.
  • Pasteurisation.
  • Fermentation.
  • Irradiation.
132. Pasteurisation
  • Pasteurisation uses controlled heat treatment to reduce harmful microorganisms.
  • It does not usually sterilise food completely.
  • It is widely used for milk.
  • The process is named after Louis Pasteur.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Pasteurisation ≠ Sterilisation.

133. Milk — Nutritional Facts
  • Milk provides high-quality protein.
  • It is a major source of calcium.
  • It provides vitamin B12.
  • Many milk products provide riboflavin.
  • Natural milk is not a rich source of iron.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Milk → Good calcium source, poor iron source.

134. Egg — Nutritional Facts
  • Egg provides high-quality complete protein.
  • Egg yolk contains fat-soluble nutrients.
  • Egg contains vitamin B12 and choline.
  • Egg contains essentially no dietary fibre.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Egg → Complete Protein, No Fibre

135. Pulses
  • Pulses are rich in plant protein.
  • They provide fibre, iron, folate and complex carbohydrates.
  • They are relatively low in methionine compared with cereals.
  • Combining pulses with cereals improves amino-acid quality.
136. Cereals

Important cereals include:

  • Rice.
  • Wheat.
  • Maize.
  • Millets.
  • Cereals are major carbohydrate sources.
  • Whole grains contain more fibre, vitamins and minerals than highly refined grains.
137. Millets

Examples include:

  • Ragi/finger millet.
  • Pearl millet/bajra.
  • Sorghum/jowar.
  • Foxtail millet.
  • Little millet.
  • Millets provide complex carbohydrates and varying amounts of fibre and minerals.
138. Ragi
  • Ragi is also called finger millet.
  • It is notable for relatively high calcium content compared with many cereals.
  • It also provides fibre.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ragi → Calcium-Rich Millet

139. Groundnut
  • Groundnut provides protein and fat.
  • It is rich in energy.
  • It contains mostly unsaturated fats.
  • It also provides niacin, vitamin E and minerals.
140. Soybean
  • Soybean is rich in protein.
  • Soy protein provides all essential amino acids.
  • It is also a source of unsaturated fat.
  • Soy products include tofu, soy milk and textured soy protein.
141. Green Leafy Vegetables
  • Green leafy vegetables provide folate.
  • They supply carotenoids.
  • Many provide non-haem iron.
  • They also supply fibre and minerals.
142. Fruits
  • Fruits provide vitamins, minerals, water and fibre.
  • Citrus fruits and guava are important vitamin C sources.
  • Orange/yellow fruits may supply beta-carotene.
  • Whole fruit generally provides more fibre than fruit juice.
143. Nuts and Seeds
  • Nuts and seeds provide healthy fats, protein, minerals and fibre.
  • Examples include groundnuts, almonds, walnuts, sesame, chia and flax.
144. Cooking and Nutrients
  • Excessive heating can destroy some heat-sensitive vitamins.
  • Vitamin C and some B vitamins are especially vulnerable.
  • Minerals are not destroyed by heat but may leach into cooking water.
  • Steaming or using minimal water can reduce nutrient loss.
145. Polished Rice and Vitamin B1
  • Heavy polishing removes the outer layers of rice.
  • These layers contain thiamine.
  • Diets dominated by highly polished rice historically contributed to beriberi.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Polished Rice → Thiamine Loss → Beriberi Risk

146. Germination
  • Germination activates enzymes in seeds.
  • It can improve digestibility.
  • Some vitamin levels may increase.
  • Sprouting can reduce certain antinutritional factors.
147. Fermentation
  • Fermentation uses microorganisms to transform food.
  • It can improve flavour, digestibility and preservation.
  • Idli and dosa batter undergo microbial fermentation.
  • Curd formation involves lactic-acid bacteria.
148. Probiotics
  • Probiotics are live microorganisms that provide health benefits when consumed in adequate amounts.
  • Certain Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains are examples.
  • Not every fermented food automatically contains clinically proven probiotic strains.
149. Prebiotics
  • Prebiotics are substrates selectively used by beneficial gut microorganisms.
  • Many prebiotics are fermentable dietary fibres.
  • They support beneficial microbial activity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Probiotic → Beneficial microorganism.

Prebiotic → Food/substrate for beneficial microorganisms.

150. Antioxidants
  • Antioxidants reduce oxidative damage by neutralising reactive species.
  • Vitamin C and vitamin E have antioxidant roles.
  • Carotenoids and many plant compounds also have antioxidant activity.
151. Free Radicals
  • Free radicals contain unpaired electrons.
  • Excess reactive oxygen species can damage lipids, proteins and DNA.
  • Normal metabolism also produces reactive oxygen species.
  • Antioxidant defence systems limit damage.
152. Glycaemic Index
  • Glycaemic index compares how rapidly carbohydrate-containing foods raise blood glucose.
  • Pure glucose is commonly assigned a reference value of 100.
  • Fibre, fat, protein, food processing and cooking influence glycaemic response.
153. Glycaemic Load
  • Glycaemic load considers both glycaemic index and the amount of available carbohydrate in a serving.
  • It better reflects the overall glucose impact of a typical portion.
154. Essential Nutrient
  • An essential nutrient cannot be synthesised by the body in sufficient quantity and therefore must be obtained from diet.
  • Essential amino acids, essential fatty acids, vitamins and certain minerals are examples.
155. Non-Essential Does Not Mean Unnecessary
  • A non-essential nutrient in biochemical terminology means the body can synthesise it.
  • It does not mean that the substance has no physiological importance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Non-essential amino acid → Body can synthesise it, not “unimportant.”

156. Nutrition in Pregnancy
  • Energy and nutrient needs increase during pregnancy.
  • Folate is especially important before conception and early pregnancy.
  • Iron requirement rises.
  • Protein and several micronutrient requirements also increase.
  • Adequate iodine supports fetal brain development.
157. Nutrition During Lactation
  • Lactation increases energy and nutrient requirements.
  • Adequate fluid intake is important.
  • Maternal nutrition supports milk production and maternal health.
158. Infant Nutrition
  • Breast milk provides nutrients and immune components.
  • Colostrum is the first milk.
  • It is rich in antibodies.
  • Exclusive breastfeeding is widely recommended for early infancy under public-health guidance, with complementary foods introduced later according to age and developmental readiness.
159. Colostrum
  • Colostrum is yellowish first milk.
  • It is rich in immunoglobulins, especially IgA.
  • It contains protein and protective factors.
  • It provides important passive immunity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Colostrum → Antibody-Rich First Milk

160. Complementary Feeding
  • Complementary feeding begins when breast milk alone can no longer meet all nutrient needs.
  • Complementary foods should be nutrient-dense, age-appropriate and hygienically prepared.
  • Breastfeeding can continue alongside complementary foods.
161. Nutritional Deficiency — Quick Table in Words
  • Protein-energy deficiency → Kwashiorkor/Marasmus.
  • Vitamin A deficiency → Night blindness.
  • Vitamin B1 deficiency → Beriberi.
  • Vitamin B3 deficiency → Pellagra.
  • Vitamin C deficiency → Scurvy.
  • Vitamin D deficiency → Rickets.
  • Vitamin K deficiency → Bleeding.
  • Iron deficiency → Anaemia.
  • Iodine deficiency → Goitre/IDD.
  • Calcium/vitamin D inadequacy → Poor bone mineralisation.
162. Important Nutrient-Source Pairs
  • Carbohydrate → Rice/wheat.
  • Protein → Pulses/egg/milk.
  • Fat → Oils/nuts/seeds.
  • Vitamin A precursor → Carrot/green leaves.
  • Vitamin C → Amla/guava/citrus.
  • Vitamin D → Sunlight exposure + selected foods.
  • Vitamin B12 → Animal foods/fortified foods.
  • Calcium → Milk/ragi/sesame.
  • Iron → Meat/pulses/green leaves.
  • Iodine → Iodised salt.
163. Important Digestion Enzyme Pairs
  • Salivary amylase → Starch.
  • Pepsin → Protein.
  • Pancreatic amylase → Starch.
  • Trypsin → Protein/peptides.
  • Lipase → Fats.
  • Maltase → Maltose.
  • Lactase → Lactose.
  • Sucrase → Sucrose.
164. TNPSC Traps
  • Carbohydrate provides about 4 kcal/g.
  • Protein provides about 4 kcal/g.
  • Fat provides about 9 kcal/g.
  • Vitamins and minerals do not directly provide calories.
  • Water provides no calories.
  • Fibre provides little directly digestible energy but has major health functions.
  • Plant storage carbohydrate → Starch.
  • Animal storage carbohydrate → Glycogen.
  • Humans cannot digest cellulose.
  • Protein consists of amino acids.
  • Cereals and pulses complement each other's amino-acid patterns.
  • Kwashiorkor is classically associated with oedema.
  • Marasmus is associated with severe wasting.
  • Fat-soluble vitamins → A, D, E, K.
  • B and C are water soluble.
  • Vitamin A → Night blindness.
  • Vitamin D → Rickets in children.
  • Vitamin E → Antioxidant.
  • Vitamin K → Clotting.
  • B1 → Thiamine → Beriberi.
  • B2 → Riboflavin.
  • B3 → Niacin → Pellagra.
  • B9 → Folate.
  • B12 → Cobalamin.
  • Vitamin C → Ascorbic acid → Scurvy.
  • Magnesium, not iron, is central in chlorophyll.
  • Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body.
  • Iron is part of haemoglobin.
  • Iodine is needed for thyroid hormones.
  • Sodium is the major extracellular cation.
  • Potassium is the major intracellular cation.
  • Excess fluoride can cause fluorosis.
  • ORS does not merely “stop diarrhoea”; it prevents/treats dehydration.
  • Bile contains no digestive enzyme.
  • Dietary fat is absorbed largely through lacteals.
  • BMI is kg/m².
  • Malnutrition includes both undernutrition and overnutrition.
  • Stunting → Low height for age.
  • Wasting → Low weight for height.
  • Underweight → Low weight for age.
  • Hidden hunger → Micronutrient deficiency.
  • Pasteurisation is not sterilisation.
  • Milk is rich in calcium but poor in iron.
  • Egg contains high-quality protein but essentially no fibre.
  • Sprouting and fermentation can improve nutrient availability.
  • Probiotic and prebiotic are different.
165. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Carb → 4 kcal.
  • Protein → 4 kcal.
  • Fat → 9 kcal.
  • Starch → Plant storage.
  • Glycogen → Animal storage.
  • Cellulose → Fibre.
  • Protein → Amino acids.
  • Kwashiorkor → Oedema.
  • Marasmus → Wasting.
  • ADEK → Fat soluble.
  • A → Vision.
  • B1 → Beriberi.
  • B3 → Pellagra.
  • B9 → Folate.
  • B12 → Cobalamin.
  • C → Scurvy.
  • D → Rickets.
  • E → Antioxidant.
  • K → Clotting.
  • Calcium → Bones.
  • Iron → Haemoglobin.
  • Iodine → Thyroid.
  • Sodium → Extracellular.
  • Potassium → Intracellular.
  • ORS → Glucose + salts.
  • Lacteal → Fat.
  • BMI → kg/m².
  • Stunting → Height/age.
  • Wasting → Weight/height.
  • Hidden hunger → Micronutrients.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What is nutrition? → Process of obtaining and using nutrients.
  • What is a balanced diet? → Diet supplying all essential nutrients in suitable amounts.
  • Main macronutrients? → Carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
  • Main micronutrients? → Vitamins and minerals.
  • Energy from carbohydrate? → About 4 kcal/g.
  • Energy from protein? → About 4 kcal/g.
  • Energy from fat? → About 9 kcal/g.
  • Does water provide calories? → No.
  • Does vitamin provide calories? → No.
  • Major blood-glucose fuel? → Glucose.
  • Common table sugar? → Sucrose.
  • Sucrose consists of? → Glucose + fructose.
  • Milk sugar? → Lactose.
  • Lactose consists of? → Glucose + galactose.
  • Plant-storage carbohydrate? → Starch.
  • Animal-storage carbohydrate? → Glycogen.
  • Plant cell-wall polysaccharide? → Cellulose.
  • Can humans digest cellulose? → No.
  • Main role of dietary fibre? → Supports bowel health and stool bulk.
  • Building blocks of protein? → Amino acids.
  • Bond joining amino acids? → Peptide bond.
  • How many essential amino acids in adults? → Nine.
  • Example of complete animal protein? → Egg.
  • Important complete plant protein? → Soy.
  • Why combine cereals and pulses? → Their amino-acid profiles complement one another.
  • Protein-energy malnutrition with oedema? → Kwashiorkor.
  • Severe wasting without typical oedema? → Marasmus.
  • Highest energy-yielding macronutrient? → Fat.
  • Triglyceride consists of? → Glycerol + three fatty acids.
  • Two essential fatty acids? → Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid.
  • Omega-6 essential fatty acid? → Linoleic acid.
  • Omega-3 essential fatty acid? → Alpha-linolenic acid.
  • Industrial trans fats generally do what? → Increase cardiovascular risk.
  • LDL commonly called? → Bad cholesterol.
  • HDL commonly called? → Good cholesterol.
  • Fat-soluble vitamins? → A, D, E, K.
  • Water-soluble vitamins? → B-complex and C.
  • Vitamin A function? → Vision and epithelial maintenance.
  • Vitamin A deficiency? → Night blindness/xerophthalmia.
  • Provitamin A pigment? → Beta-carotene.
  • Vitamin D main function? → Calcium/phosphate absorption and bone mineralisation.
  • Vitamin D deficiency in children? → Rickets.
  • Vitamin D deficiency in adults? → Osteomalacia.
  • Vitamin E main role? → Antioxidant.
  • Vitamin K role? → Blood clotting.
  • Vitamin B1 name? → Thiamine.
  • B1 deficiency? → Beriberi.
  • Vitamin B2? → Riboflavin.
  • Vitamin B3? → Niacin.
  • B3 deficiency? → Pellagra.
  • Classic pellagra 3Ds? → Dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia.
  • Vitamin B6? → Pyridoxine.
  • Vitamin B7? → Biotin.
  • Vitamin B9? → Folate/folic acid.
  • Why is folate important in pregnancy? → Helps prevent neural-tube defects.
  • Vitamin B12? → Cobalamin.
  • Metal present in B12? → Cobalt.
  • Protein required for B12 absorption? → Intrinsic factor.
  • Main B12 absorption site? → Terminal ileum.
  • B12 deficiency causes? → Megaloblastic anaemia and possible neurological damage.
  • Vitamin C chemical name? → Ascorbic acid.
  • Vitamin C deficiency? → Scurvy.
  • Vitamin C helps synthesis of? → Collagen.
  • Vitamin C improves absorption of? → Non-haem iron.
  • Rich vitamin C sources? → Amla, guava and citrus fruits.
  • Most abundant mineral in human body? → Calcium.
  • Main storage site of calcium? → Bones and teeth.
  • Mineral in haemoglobin? → Iron.
  • Iron deficiency causes? → Anaemia.
  • Vitamin improving non-haem iron absorption? → Vitamin C.
  • Iodine required for? → Thyroid hormones.
  • Iodine deficiency commonly causes? → Goitre.
  • Major extracellular cation? → Sodium.
  • Major intracellular cation? → Potassium.
  • Mineral associated with dental-caries prevention? → Fluoride.
  • Excess fluoride causes? → Fluorosis.
  • ORS full form? → Oral Rehydration Solution.
  • ORS contains? → Glucose and electrolytes in water.
  • Why does ORS work? → Glucose-assisted sodium absorption draws water into the body.
  • Where does carbohydrate digestion begin? → Mouth.
  • Salivary enzyme for starch? → Salivary amylase.
  • Where does protein digestion begin significantly? → Stomach.
  • Stomach protein enzyme? → Pepsin.
  • Where does most fat digestion occur? → Small intestine.
  • Substance emulsifying fats? → Bile salts.
  • Enzyme digesting triglycerides? → Lipase.
  • Where are most nutrients absorbed? → Small intestine.
  • What absorbs most dietary fats? → Lacteals.
  • BMR stands for? → Basal Metabolic Rate.
  • BMI formula? → Weight in kg ÷ height² in metres.
  • BMI unit? → kg/m².
  • General adult normal BMI range? → 18.5–24.9.
  • Does BMI directly measure body-fat percentage? → No.
  • Malnutrition means only undernutrition? → No.
  • Stunting means? → Low height for age.
  • Wasting means? → Low weight for height.
  • Underweight means? → Low weight for age.
  • Hidden hunger means? → Micronutrient deficiency despite sufficient or near-sufficient calories.
  • Common nutritional cause of anaemia? → Iron deficiency.
  • Classic food-fortification example? → Iodised salt.
  • What is pasteurisation? → Controlled heating to reduce harmful microorganisms.
  • Does pasteurisation sterilise milk completely? → No.
  • Milk is particularly rich in? → Calcium and high-quality protein.
  • Milk is a poor source of? → Iron.
  • Egg provides? → High-quality complete protein.
  • Does egg contain dietary fibre? → Essentially no.
  • Pulses are good sources of? → Protein, fibre, folate and minerals.
  • Ragi is notable for? → Relatively high calcium content.
  • Heavy rice polishing removes which important vitamin? → Thiamine/B1.
  • Deficiency historically associated with polished-rice diets? → Beriberi.
  • Curd formation involves? → Lactic-acid bacteria.
  • Probiotic means? → Beneficial live microorganism consumed in adequate amount.
  • Prebiotic means? → Substrate that supports beneficial gut microorganisms.
  • First milk after childbirth? → Colostrum.
  • Colostrum is rich in? → Antibodies, especially IgA.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Carb 4, Protein 4, Fat 9; ADEK fat-soluble; A → night blindness; B1 → beriberi; B3 → pellagra; C → scurvy; D → rickets; Iron → anaemia; Iodine → goitre.
